step1_summary: Chief complaint: 1-week history of sore throat followed by a dry cough

Symptom chronology/character:
  • Day 0–1: Sore throat began (Thursday/Friday of last week)
  • Day 1–2: Dry, non-productive cough started
  • Day 3–4: Developed mild exertional shortness of breath, occasional wheeze, and some chest discomfort
  • First 3 days: Subjective fever; now afebrile
  • Intermittent headaches
  • Reduced appetite but no weight loss
  • Course is ‘up-and-down’—periods of improvement then worsening
  • No sputum, haemoptysis, nasal congestion, sinus symptoms, rash
Aggravating/alleviating factors: SOB only with exertion (still able to exercise and climb stairs); cough not worse at night; no specific relieving factors reported
Past medical history: None; specifically no asthma, no thromboembolic disease
Family history: Mother had lung cancer; no family clotting disorders reported
Social history: Non-smoker (only experimented once or twice), no known asbestos exposure, lives in UK >12 yrs, recent travel limited to Europe; working adult who required sick leave 2 days this week
Physical exam: Not performed (remote consult); patient feels no neck lumps

V: Pulmonary embolism: Acute dry cough, exertional dyspnoea, and chest pain can be PE, although risk factors are minimal
I: Acute viral upper respiratory infection / viral bronchitis: Classic sequence of sore throat → dry cough with low-grade fever
COVID-19 infection: Presents with sore throat, dry cough, fever, headache, appetite loss, fluctuating course
Atypical (mycoplasma/chlamydia) pneumonia: Dry cough, low-grade fever, headache, chest discomfort
N: Lung malignancy: Cough and chest pain with family history, but very acute onset and no weight loss make it less likely
D: COPD exacerbation: Would explain cough and SOB but patient is young and non-smoker
A: Allergic/reactive airway disease (new-onset asthma): Wheeze, exertional SOB, dry cough that is non-productive
T: Inhalation irritation (smoke/chemical) causing acute bronchitis—no exposure reported
E: Thyroid enlargement causing cough/SOB—no neck swelling, unlikely

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Acute viral upper respiratory infection / viral bronchitis (non-COVID)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic 1-week viral prodrome of sore throat, low-grade fever, progressing to dry cough; fluctuating improvement; typical duration; no red-flag findings
supporting_evidence: Onset with sore throat and low-grade fever
No focal lung findings, purulent sputum, or severe systemic illness
opposing_evidence: Presence of exertional SOB and wheeze could suggest lower airway involvement (e.g., asthma) or COVID-19

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Symptom constellation (sore throat, dry cough, fever, headache, appetite loss, variable course) is highly consistent with COVID-19; prevalence still significant
supporting_evidence: Dry cough, sore throat, fever and headache
Fluctuating (‘up-and-down’) course typical of many COVID cases
opposing_evidence: No confirmed exposure or positive test

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Dry cough with wheeze and exertional dyspnoea, no nocturnal predominance yet; viral infection could have triggered first presentation
supporting_evidence: Exertional shortness of breath but able to exercise (suggests airway limitation rather than parenchymal disease)
opposing_evidence: No past history of asthma or allergies apart from peanuts
No clear pattern of triggers or nocturnal worsening

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Dry cough, low fevers, headache, mild chest pain can signal atypical pneumonia, but overall mild illness and improving trend make it less likely
opposing_evidence: No persistent fever, no systemic toxicity

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: PE causes acute SOB and chest pain, but patient’s symptoms are mild, with no risk factors (immobility, OCP, recent surgery, clot history); cough and sore throat began first, which is atypical
